contraindications: Valproate in women of childbearing potential: major teratogen (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental disorders); avoid unless no alternative exists.
interactions: Levetiracetam + hydroxychloroquine, prednisone or amlodipine: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; levetiracetam is renally cleared, so dose by creatinine clearance.
Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + prednisone: CYP3A4 induction lowers prednisolone exposure; may need a higher steroid dose.
Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + amlodipine: CYP3A4 induction lowers amlodipine levels; IV loading adds hypotension and arrhythmia risk.
Nicardipine or labetalol + amlodipine: additive hypotension; titrate the infusion to the blood pressure target.
Lacosamide + labetalol: additive PR prolongation and bradycardia; obtain an ECG before loading.
Hydroxychloroquine + other QT-prolonging drugs: additive QT prolongation.
output.proposed: Lorazepam, a second-line antiseizure medication (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate or lacosamide) and IV nicardipine or labetalol with hydroxychloroquine, prednisone, amlodipine and vitamin D
warnings: Hydroxychloroquine can lower the seizure threshold (labelled warning).

output.query: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome with seizures: blood pressure management and status epilepticus treatment

results.finding: PRES presents with headache, encephalopathy, seizures and visual disturbance, with bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic edema on MRI.
Treatment is removal of the trigger and controlled blood pressure lowering, by about 25% in the first hours; most patients recover clinically and radiologically.
Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine.
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective second-line agents for benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus.

output.summary: PRES presents with headache, encephalopathy, seizures and visual disturbance and shows bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic edema on MRI; it is treated by removing the trigger and lowering blood pressure in a controlled way, and usually reverses [Fugate_2015]. Status epilepticus is treated with a benzodiazepine and then a second-line agent [Glauser_2016; ESETT_2019].

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT load valproate in this 42-year-old woman of reproductive age: teratogen risk
Do NOT give fosphenytoin without continuous cardiac and blood pressure monitoring during the infusion
Do NOT lower BP precipitously: risks ischemic injury in PRES
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Lower blood pressure with a titratable IV agent (nicardipine infusion or labetalol boluses) by no more than 25% in the first hour, then towards 160/100 mm Hg over the next hours; do not over-correct [Fugate_2015].
Load a second-line ASM: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (maximum 4500 mg), and avoid valproate because she is of reproductive age and valproate is a major teratogen [ESETT_2019].
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].
Involve rheumatology and nephrology for the lupus flare with active nephritis (RBC casts, protein:creatinine 1.8) to plan immunosuppression and renal biopsy.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

accepted: Non-convulsive status epilepticus secondary to posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) from hypertensive emergency in active SLE

differential.key_features: Active SLE (dsDNA 42, low C3 and C4, nephritis) raises it, but MRI shows a posterior vasogenic PRES pattern and CSF shows only minimal nonspecific change
Blood pressure 172/108 can cause encephalopathy, but MRI shows the imaging-defined PRES pattern

differential.diagnosis: Breakthrough seizures from low levetiracetam level
differential.key_features: Levetiracetam 8 mcg/mL is low and contributory, but does not explain the headache, hypertension or posterior MRI pattern
No diffusion restriction on MRI, serum and CSF neuronal antibodies negative, CSF without inflammation
Prednisone 30 mg daily may have contributed to the blood pressure rise that triggered PRES; the steroid itself does not cause status epilepticus

key_clinical_evidence: PRES classically presents with seizures, encephalopathy, visual symptoms, and severe hypertension; bilateral posterior parieto-occipital vasogenic FLAIR hyperintensity is characteristic but not specific [Fugate_2015]
Active SLE expands the differential to lupus cerebritis and antiphospholipid-related events, but PRES is the unifying diagnosis here
A low ASM level, PRES and a lupus flare are concurrent precipitants; all three must be addressed
Avoid valproate in women of reproductive age; use levetiracetam preferentially

patient.history_present_illness: A 42-year-old Asian female teacher was brought to the emergency department by her husband after a witnessed brief generalized convulsion at home. Her husband reports she had been complaining of a severe headache for three days and had been 'not herself' — forgetting words mid-sentence and seeming confused about the day of the week. She had one previous unprovoked seizure 6 months ago. The shaking episode lasted approximately 2 minutes then stopped on its own, but she did not regain her normal level of consciousness. When EMS arrived 8 minutes after the seizure, she was awake but confused, answering questions with inappropriate words, and appeared agitated. In the ED she is minimally following commands, oriented only to her name. She has a history of SLE diagnosed 6 years ago, in clinical remission per her rheumatologist until a joint flare 10 days ago. She takes hydroxychloroquine and a prednisone taper started 10 days ago for the joint flare, currently 30 mg daily on day 10. She also takes levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily started 5 months ago after a first unprovoked seizure. Her blood pressure at home has been elevated per recent records. No fevers, no sick contacts, no recent travel.
